en: The *Vajrajvālodayā-sādhanopāyikā* by Ānandagarbha (ff.
170r6–186r3 in Göttingen Xc 14/39) refers to his Śaiva Age, a version received on 2009.03.02.
Homage to the glorious Hevajra.
Having paid homage to Śrī Heruka, the all-pervading Lord who subdues those difficult to tame,
I shall explain this *Vajrajvālodayā*, which is essential for the practice of sādhana.

In that regard, according to the ritual procedure of the *Ārya-sarvabuddhasamāyoga-tantra*, a yogin who has obtained the pledges (*samaya*) and so forth in the maṇḍala of Śrī Heruka, whose mind is purified by the constant observance of those prescribed pledges, and who is clothed in variegated garments— residing in a cremation ground, a temple, a shrine of the Mothers, or similar locations, and always holding the vajra and bell— he shall accomplish supreme siddhi. (Paramādya, D 225v)

Having placed before oneself the maṇḍala of the glorious Heruka— whether in the form of a painted image, a cast metal statue, or otherwise— as a great means of summoning all [beings], one should think:
"For the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings, may I become the glorious Heruka."
Having thus generated the mind,
one should produce an eight-petalled lotus at the throat with the syllable *hrīḥ*, and on the petal of the tongue-lotus, a white five-pronged vajra with the syllable *hūṃ*;
this is called the "vajra-tongue."

One should remain thus. Having visualized two moon-maṇḍalas from the two *akāra*s in the two hands, and above them two five-pronged vajras from the two *hūṃ* syllables, one should turn back [the visualization] by means of the *hūṃ* syllable itself, [the fingers] having the form of vajras with needle-like points.
"Oṃ sarvaviśuddhidharmatāvajra sidhya hūṃ.
Having thus formed the vajrapadma mudrā, one should rotate it seven times.
In this way, even that which is impure shall become pure.

Having formed the vajra-bind, one should bend the two index fingers so that their backs are joined together; having inserted them inside by way of a needle, and having raised the needle formed by the joining of the two thumbs, one should hold it face upward above the cross-legged posture—this is the Vajrapadmā.
Oṃ vajracakra hūṃ.

Having bound this *vajracakrā* like a whirling firebrand (*ālātacakra*) through the practice of circumambulating to the right, and having thereby manifested the mandala of Śrī Heruka, one should again place it within the mouth and gaze upon it eight times.
One should recite: *Oṃ vajracakra hūṃ*. Thus, one enters the maṇḍala of Śrī Heruka. Having formed the two vajra-fists, [one performs] the bodhyagrya-vajra-bind.
She is renowned as Vajracakrā, the accomplisher of all maṇḍalas.
Then, if possible, one should worship that maṇḍala with flowers and other offerings.

Reciting, "Oṃ, with the prostration of the vajra of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas, I perform the vajra-salutation," and having prostrated with the five-pointed salutation (*pañcamaṇḍalaka*) toward the three directions,
[one should do so] with a compassionate and humble mind.
I go for refuge to the Sugata, who possesses faultless intellect, whose delusion regarding the entire body has been destroyed,
and who stands at the center of the lotuses of all lineages.
Because it is the source for those of superior intelligence and because it strikes fear into the base,
I have gone for refuge to the Dharma, which is the Victor’s Grove.
He becomes one skilled in cultivation,
whose mind possesses vast compassion, whose intellect is awakened, and who removes the poison of the serpents of passion and the like.
I go for refuge to the host of lords of ascetics, who have transcended the cycle of existence.
Having taken the triple refuge and bound the vajra, one should generate the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*).

Oṃ! I generate the supreme great bodhicitta of all Tathāgatas for the sake of protecting, benefiting, and bringing happiness to the entire realm of sentient beings without exception, as a sign of the attainment of the highest siddhi; for the sake of ultimate mastery over the perfection of existence, up to the mastery over the sovereignty of the supreme great siddhi.
Then, by means of the application of reflections and so forth, one should perform the binding of the mudrā. In this regard, the binding of the mudrā is as follows:
forming the *saṃpuṭāñjali* (the hollowed-palms gesture), one should say this:
"All phenomena are mutually interpenetrating" means that all phenomena are mutually entered, like the *vajrāñjali* mudrā formed by the mutual joining of fingers.
"Vajrāñjali" refers to the firm vajra-binding;
all phenomena have entered into it completely.
Regarding "vajrabandha":
then one should burst open the vajra-bind at the heart with "Vajrabandha trāt" three times, and [recite] "vajrāveśa."

Having bound the Great Seal of the Vajra-Entrance (*vajrāveśamahāmudrā*) and uttering the syllable *aḥ*, one causes the sharp Vajra of Wrath—the Vajra of the Vajra Family composed of atoms, consisting of blue flames, blazing with a mass of radiant light, and possessing five prongs—to enter from the region of space into one’s own heart.
"Stay, O Vajra! Be firm for me; be eternal for me; [be] in my heart and in my intentions; grant me all success, HŪṂ PHAṬ HA HA HA HA HO! Having thus made the descent firm, this is the "Vajra-fist."
Having bound the Vajramuṣṭi-samayamudrā,
one should recite "Oṃ vajramuṣṭi baṃ" three times.
In the vajrabandha, having inserted the two thumbs between one's own little fingers and ring fingers, one should hold them;
this is the samaya-mudrā of vajrāveśa.
Then, by bending both index fingers of this very [mudrā] and joining them with one's own thumbs, one should press the backs of those two thumbs with them;
this is the Vajramuṣṭi-samayamudrā.

Then, having placed the syllable *hūṃ* in the center of the Wrath-Vajra (*krodhavajra*) residing within one’s own heart, one should meditate upon the selflessness of all phenomena, which is luminous by nature.
Then, with that very same *hūṃ*, accompanied by the sixteen vowels, one should contemplate one’s own mind as a moon disc in the form of a reflection.

Above that, again with that same *hūṃ*, there is a second moon disc transformed from the syllables beginning with *ka* and ending with *pa*, together with the *hūṃ*-syllable and the Wrath-Vajra. Having mentally inscribed the *hūṃ*-syllable in the center of the vajra:

"Just as the sentient being, so the mudrā; just as the mudrā, so indeed I"—by means of this meditation on Vajrahūṃkāra, having emanated a vajra consisting of the entire vajra-family, and having transformed the realm of all sentient beings into that very nature, one should mentally cause them to enter into that vajra. Then, through the yoga of empowering the sentient beings, having generated oneself as Vajrasattva while uttering "I am Vajrasattva! I am Vajrasattva!", and once again brandishing the vajra with pride, one should speak thus:
"I am Vajrasattva.
In this regard, the yoga of the empowerment of the sentient being is as follows:
"Indeed, the sentient being is the self of all; he dwells within my own self as well. [5]
"In essence, he is Vajrasattva; O Omniscient One, enter into me! Having thus contemplated oneself as Śrī Heruka through the pride of being Vajrasattva, one should say:
"I am the Mahāsamayasattva."
Thus. Then, having bound the *samayamudrā* of Śrī Heruka, one should say: "I am the *samaya*.
With that very *samayamudrā*, one should empower oneself at the heart, the *ūrṇā* (between the eyebrows), the throat, and the head.
"O Samayasattva, please empower me!
Then, reciting that mantra from one's own heart, one should properly bind the great mudrā (mahāmudrā) of that deity;
thereafter, one should perform the recitation (jāpa) or the meditative cultivation (bhāvanā).
Thus [ends] this [work] useful for the practice of the Mother of Yoga.
If he wishes to perform the subsequent application,

having performed the yoga just described and having bound the Blessed One’s Mahāmudrā, he should produce a double-lotus (*viśvapadma*) in the space in front by means of the syllable *hrīḥ*; above that, he should visualize a five-pronged blazing vajra with the syllables *huṃ* and *aḥ*.
Then one should cultivate the vajra-egoity, thinking:
"I am the blazing vajra, HŪṂ.
Then, one should visualize that vajra as oneself, Śrī Heruka.
"I am Śrī Heruka, HŪṂ."
Then, having drawn Śrī Heruka to that very place, caused him to enter, bound him, and brought him under control with these heart-mantras accompanied by their mudrās:
Vajrāṅkuśi jaḥ!
Vajrapāśe hūṃ!
Vajraśṛṅkhalā: BAṂ;
Vajraghaṇṭā: HOḤ.
In this regard, these are the mudrās characterized by mutual non-existence.

Having formed two wrathful fists (*krodhamuṣṭi*), with the right upper hand forming a "arm-knot" (*bāhugranthi*), the index finger extended is the "Vajra-commander" (*vajrājñākārī*). With that [finger], one performs the gestures for Vajrāṅkuśī as a hook (*aṅkuśī*), for Pāśā as a binding of the arm-knot, for Sphoṭā as the pressing of the knot, and for Ghaṇṭā as a subtle sounding at one's own heart.
"With the *tripatākā*, the tips of the *khaṭaka*, the *pāśa*, and the *līlā* gestures, together with the *ahimokṣaṇa* [snakes-unleashing] movements,
and with the tips whirled like flashing lightning— this is known as the *vajranṛtyā*.
Thus is the definition of *vajranṛtyā*.
Having formed two vajra-fists and extended the two index fingers, one should hold them joined separately;
this is the characteristic of the wrathful fist (*krodhamuṣṭi*).
Then, having bound the pledge-mudrā (*samayamudrā*) of Śrī Heruka...
Uttering "haḥ haḥ haḥ haḥ rulu rulu huḍ asyeti," one should cause the Blessed One to become visible.
Having seen him, one should manifest that Jñānasattva within one's own body.
Having drawn [the deity] forth, caused to enter, bound, and brought under control, one should accomplish the practice.

With the mantra "haḥ haḥ haḥ haḥ rulu rulu hūṃ," which is the heart-mantra of Śrī Heruka, using the secret hook together with the bell and the two middle hooks, one should draw one's own heart [to the deity].

Then, having bound the *śrīheruka-samayamudrā* and uttering "Thou art the pledge, Hīḥ," one should, at dawn, having completed the mandala from behind, meditate upon oneself as Śrī Heruka, who has become one with Śrī Heruka entered [into the mandala].
"Thou art the pledge, I am [the pledge]. *Jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ haḥ haḥ haḥ haḥ rulu rulu hūṃ*. One should recite this three times.
He has four faces and eight arms;
among them, the first face is wrathful,
and the second face on the right is joyful with intense passion.
Behind is the third, the eating face;
to the left is the fourth, the amorous face.
And this has been indicated by the song of the four faces.
With two arms, by way of holding a wind-cloth, he wears a moist human skin.
With two [hands] he holds a bow and arrow;
with the third on the right, he is intent on brandishing a three-pronged trident blazing with vajras; and with the fourth, he holds a skull-cup filled with great blood.
With the third left hand, he holds a vajra-khaṭvāṅga together with a bell;
with the fourth, he holds a skull-cup filled with human flesh (mahāmāṃsa).
Alternatively, he may have two arms and one face.

On his left shoulder, in the manner of a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), he rests a *khaṭvāṅga* staff topped with a bell and a vajra. With his right hand, marked by the triple-bannered gesture (*tripatākā*), he holds a five-pronged blazing vajra;
with his left hand, he holds a skull-cup filled with human flesh (*mahāmāṃsa*).
Wearing a crown of skulls with the Buddha as the crest-jewel,
seated upon a high universal lotus throne,
he places his left foot on the ground and positions his right foot in the *sattvaparyaṅka* posture.
Having placed the sole of that [foot] upon the left thigh by means of the yoga of encasement,

[he visualizes himself as] one whose hair is ablaze, possessing a mandala of light with red flames consisting of blue-flaming vajras, resembling the fierce fire of the cremation ground at the time of the great dissolution.
With the various movements of the face resulting from the combination of sentiments such as the Furious (raudra) and others.
"With a gaze made to dance by a look blazing with playful eyebrows and frowns.
Then, having sealed [the practitioner] with the great mudrās of the Dharma and Karma, and having bound the Samāja-mudrā, [one utters]: JAḤ HŪṂ VAṂ HOḤ.
Setting it in motion through the mind by means of virtuous application, one should cause all the Tathāgatas to enter one's own body and accomplish [the practice] with the samaya-mudrās.

Having bound the Great Seal (mahāmudrā) of the Vajradhātu and formed the Samaya Seal of Vairocana with it, one should recite three times: "Jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ! You are the samaya; you are the samaya; I am the samaya, O Vajradhātu! In this way, they become accomplished.
Having bound the vajra-vajra and made the *sattvavajrā* firm, with the middle fingers raised and joined like a sprout,
the second [mudrā] is described by the Buddhas through the contraction of the space between the middle fingers.
The middle finger and thumb joined like a jewel is the Padmasaṃkoca-madhyamā;
the fifth is the Buddha-mudrā, likewise with the tips [of the fingers] bent. These are the samaya-mudrās of all the Tathāgatas.
One should contemplate "Vajrajñāna" upon the tongues of the Tathāgatas; this is their Dharma-seal (dharmamudrā).
Having formed two vajra-fists, the left vajra-finger is grasped by the right as it is raised up;
this is the action-seal (*karmamudrā*) of Vairocana. [2]

One should hold the left vajra-fist at the heart in the manner of grasping the corner of a robe. From the right fist, with the fingers extended straight, there are the ritual gestures (*abhinaya*) of touching the earth, granting boons, and granting fearlessness; these are the action seals (*karmamudrā*) of Akṣobhya, Ratnasaṃbhava, and Amoghasiddhi.
For Amitābha, however, they are both straight and relaxed.
"Vajradhātu" is the general heart-mantra for the action seals.
Furthermore, by means of this very heart-mantra, the great mudrās together with their symbols should be employed; they arise from the two vajra-fists,
and [the left hand] is raised up by the right hand grasping the vajra-finger of the left.

The great seal (*mahāmudrā*) of the Blessed One Vairocana is formed by joining the tips of the fingers in the gesture of meditative concentration (*samādhyagrā*). That of Akṣobhya is the earth-touching gesture (*bhūsparśā*); likewise, that of Ratnasambhava is the boon-granting gesture (*varada*). For Amitābha and [Amitāyus], it is the gesture of meditative concentration; for Amoghasiddhi, it is the gesture bestowing fearlessness (*abhayapradā*). Then, with the Trailokyavijaya mudrā, one should touch the heart, the *ūrṇā* [between the eyebrows], the throat, and the crown of the head.
Oṃ śumbha niśumbha huṃ gṛhṇa 2 huṃ gṛhṇāpaya 2 huṃ ānaya hoḥ bhagavan vidyārāja huṃ phaṭ! Adhitiṣṭha mām!
Thus, one should empower oneself at the heart, the *ūrṇā* (between the eyebrows), the throat, and the head. Having formed the vajra [mudrā], the little fingers are bound as hooks (*aṅkuśa*).
This is the one called Trilokavijayā, which is to be performed with the threatening gesture and arises from two vajra-fists.
Furthermore, having bound the Ārya-Avajra, O Vajrasattva, empower it; then, one should produce a five-pronged blazing vajra at the heart.
Having generated the Vajraratna at the location of the *ūrṇā*,
the Vajradharma at the location of the throat,
and the Viśvavajra at the head as the Vajrakarma;

Oṃ Vajrasattva, maintain your pledge! O Vajrasattva, abide here with me! Be firm for me, be well-pleased with me, be well-nourished by me, be devoted to me! Grant me all accomplishments, and in all activities, make my mind auspicious! Hūṃ ha ha ha ha hoḥ! O Blessed One, Vajra of all Tathāgatas, do not abandon me! Become vajra-like, O Great Samaya-being! Āḥ!

Having thus stabilized [the rite] three times with the hundred-syllable mantra, and having bowed to the Blessed One with the *palita-vajrāñjali* (the "gray-haired vajra-palms" gesture), one should receive the complete consecration (*sarvābhiṣeka*). Therein, first, for the consecration of the skull-cup, the forehead-buddha, the crest-jewel, and the crown: utter "HŪṂ ABHIṢIÑCA MI," and then the mudrā is as follows.

With all the fingers joined at their inner sides and all the tips joined at the face, covered by the vajras of the thumbs, it reaches the cavities of the nose and eyes; and likewise upon the crown of the head, the forehead, the two sides, and the back. (9.397) [6]

Wearing a crown of skulls with the Buddha as its crest-jewel, blazing, one should not bind [the hair] with a cloth-band; rather, having performed graceful and forceful releases and the hanging down of the cloth, one should secure it firmly with a *tāla* [measure]. (9.399–400)
*Vajrapuṣpa hoḥ*. With the *tālahṛdaya* [mantra] *āḥ*, one should manifest the venerable Vairocana as a crest-jewel (*cūḍāmaṇi*), golden in color and established in the *bodhyagrī* mudrā.
Again, with the *śrīherukavajra* mudrā, one should receive the consecration of the vajra-garland (*vajramālā*), saying: "Consecrate me with the root mantra. In this regard, the mudrā is as follows:
With the hands well-extended, one should form the sharp Vajra-mudrā by binding the two tips together with the middle fingers and thumbs facing outward;
having turned it and then cast it forth, one should fix it upon the brow with a frown.
Success is achieved; all sovereignty, without exception or remainder, is fully established. Then, uttering "Huṃ Haṃ," one should bind the *kabaṇḍha* with both vajra-fists:
two [fingers] on the head, two on the forehead, two on the sides, and two from behind.
One should fasten the vajra-garland as well as the Buddha-cūḍāmaṇi;
having bound it with a silk band, with graceful and playful movements of release, one should hang the cloth and make it firm by means of a clapper.
Thus [it is said]. That very thing is the heart of the *tāla* tree.
Then, one should grasp the vajra produced from the syllable *hūṃ* with this [mantra].
"Oṃ, I consecrate you with all the vajras, hoḥ! O Blessed Vajradhara!
Then, having placed that vajra upon the head, one should receive the name-consecration:
"O Śrī Karuṇābalakrodhavajra, O Name-Vajra, be successful! You are the pledge (samaya). Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! Svasti! Namaḥ svāhā!"
And by this, one should take up the vow of the Siddhivajra:
"This is that state of omniscience, the Vajra of the Vajradhara;
you too must always maintain it as the great vow of the Vajradhara."

Thus, this is that supreme great bodhicitta of all the Tathāgatas; because of its renunciation and its constant retention, it is the ultimate secret. O Lord of Vajra-pride, *dhīḥ* is *śrīḥ*, [the essence of] woman.

Thus: as before, having placed a vajra upon the tongue and mentally inscribed the syllables of the Dharma, one should then form the *karmamudrā*, reciting [the mantra] with steadfastness from this [mudrā]. Then one should form the *mahāmudrā*. Then, having gathered the paths by means of the fourfold [set] beginning with the weapons of the wrathful deities (*krodha*), and having again formed the *mahāmudrā*, one should grasp the vajra according to its true nature (*tattva*). Passion is eternally born as wrath; Vajrasattva is the subduer.
The vajra-flame, like the fire of the sun, is indeed the supreme dissolution.
This is the reality. One should ring the bell with the left hand. Arisen from the syllable *A*, it has the characteristic of space; all space is indeed without characteristics.
One who is joined in the equality of space shall swiftly accomplish everything. (Paramādya D 235r)

The Dharma: by means of the pledge (*samaya*), one should empower the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*). Speaking "all space" through the yoga of the pinnacle of all space, one may even consume the three worlds when they are sealed with the Vajra-seals.
Thus is the convention.
Having thus accomplished oneself and remaining in the expanse of space, [one should contemplate]:
"The letter A is the gateway to all phenomena, because they are unproduced from the very beginning."

Thus, mentally inflaming [the visualization], one should contemplate that all world-systems are equal to space. Then, by means of the syllable *yaṃ*, one visualizes a wind-maṇḍala; above that, by means of the syllable *vaṃ*, a water-maṇḍala; and above that as well, by means of the syllable *laṃ*, a golden maṇḍala. Again, above that, one visualizes a water-maṇḍala by means of the syllable *va*. Upon that blazing golden maṇḍala, by means of the seed-syllables *hūṃ suṃ hūṃ* joined together, one visualizes the great Mount Meru, square-shaped and composed of the four jewels, adorned with all kinds of gems, and surrounded by the seven mountain ranges and so forth.

Reciting "Oṃ, be firm for me, O Vajra; protect all, svāhā," and touching the surface of the earth with the vajra-bind, one should begin from within [the center] a wind-maṇḍala in the shape of a half-moon, adorned with eight pillars by means of the syllable *ha*, square and surrounded by a garland of vajras. In the places of all the deities, there are viśvapadma seats by means of the syllable *hrīḥ*.
Then, having descended from the intermediate space into the inner maṇḍala, one should sit properly upon the lotus seat in the central square with the mahāmudrā and the syllable *hūṃ*.
The union with Śrī Vajrasattva, with lips firmly pressed together,
bearing the left-hand pride, the glorious one clearly manifests the gestures of the wheels of the directions;
having presided over the nether, upper, and middle realms (bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svaḥ), he shall seal them.

Consisting of all the Buddhas, it is accomplished and difficult for the evil-minded to enter. With a wrathful gaze, by means of the *vālīḍha* posture, while brandishing the right vajra, one performs the binding of the directions, the boundary, and the protection of the ground. In this manner, the enclosure wall and the cage of the mandala should be constructed.

Then, having consecrated the *argha* offering with the heart-mantra using the *vajrāñjali* gesture characterized by the *argha-mudrā*, and having consecrated the flowers, incense, lamps, and perfumes with the mudrās and mantras for the flowers and so forth; having recited the mantra over the food starting with the letter *A*; and having again formed the *mahāmudrā*, standing in the midst of the assembly of all Buddhas, one should slowly and repeatedly rotate the *utthāpanī* and the syllable *HŪṂ*.
Then, having emanated the Śrī Heruka-vajra from the blazing vajra at one’s own heart, and from the blazing sun of one’s own radiance...

Having emanated the entire host of Śrī-Gaurī and the other Vajra-Ḍākinīs with blazing hair standing erect, a mandala shining with red flames resembling the fierce fire of the cremation ground at the time of the great dissolution, wrathful, wearing a crown of a single skull and a single Buddha, and bearing their own respective emblems, one should settle them in their proper places.
*Haḥ haḥ haḥ haḥ rulu rulu hūṃ*—this is the general heart-mantra. In this regard, there is this song for raising [them]:
The pledge (samaya), having attained the state of space through the constant arising of the supreme yoga of emptiness,
causes the Sugatas to arise as the Sugata.
"O Śrīvajrasattva, you are fortunate; I am [you]"— this very song, when sung, indeed [awakens] those who have attained ultimate parinirvāṇa.
One might raise up the dead once more, how much more so those who are subject to rebirth?
Therefore,
this [teaching], which is joined with the certain path and adorned by cessation, [should be followed].
Or else, one should recite it.

With his own mantra, "Oṃ Heruka vajrasamaya hīḥ sarvaduṣṭasamayamudrāprabhañjaka hūṃ phaṭ," one should install Śrī Heruka; oneself in that place. With "Hūṃ vajraguhye siddhi paramayogeśvari hrīḥ," [one installs] Gaurī.
*Huṃ huṃ vajracaṇḍeśvari khaṭvāṅgi mahāvajri kapālamālāmukuṭe rulu rulu huṃ*—thus is Caurī. *Huṃ vajranārāyaṇi jhir ati pramohām*.
*Huṃ vajrapatāke jjir*—thus is Vetālī.
HŪṂ VAJRAPRAHARAṆI MAḌ—thus [is the mantra of] Pukkasī; HŪṂ VAJRAŚŪLĀGRI BHINDA MAḌ—thus [is the mantra of] Caṇḍālī; HŪṂ VAJRAKOŚE CCHI MAḌ—thus [is the mantra of] Ghasmarī.
HŪṂ VAJRAMALAPĀŚE MAḌ—thus is the placement of Heruka. HE VAJRA RATI MĀM—thus is the holder of the sharp arrow-dhāraṇī. VAṂ MAHĀRATAVAJRI HOR—thus is Khaṭvāṅginī, the holder [of the staff].
Oṃ vajralocane yaṃ—thus she who holds a wheel;
raṃ mahāśrīvajri hrīḥ—thus she who holds a bell and a variegated banner.
"O Vajra-flower," thus [he offers] the flowers.
With "O Vajradhūpa," [he offers] incense.
Āṃ Vajrāloke—thus [is the mantra] for the lamps.
Aḥ vajragandhe—thus are the perfumes.
Oṃ vajrāṅkuśi jaḥ! Thus [is the mantra] for the horse.
Oṃ vajrapāśe hūṃ—thus is Vajramukhī. [3] Oṃ vajrasaṅkāle baṃ—thus is Vajrālokā.
Oṃ vajraghaṇṭe hor! With this, one should install Bhasmapralayavetālī by means of her own mantra, or else the host [of deities] joined with that yoga.

There, in the inner square of the maṇḍala of Śrī Heruka—or for that practitioner—within that very square, in the eastern direction, is Gaurī. She is white in color, with a peaceful gaze and a gentle countenance; simultaneously, she casts down four great severed heads with sharp arrows drawn from her bow, and she stands in the *pratyālīḍha* posture.

And on the right is Caurī, red in color, with a face and gaze of wrath; she holds a *khaṭvāṅga* on her left shoulder by way of the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*). She wears a crown of garlands of skulls, and with her left hand in the "wrathful fist" (*krodhamuṣṭi*), she holds a goad at her heart. With the middle finger of her right hand, she brandishes an eight-spoked wheel. With her left foot, she tramples upon the three worlds.

In the west is Pramohā, with the face of the primordial Varāha, possessing the gaze of delusion; she is black, four-armed, holds a skull-cup filled with wine in her left hand, and a vajra in her right hand. Furthermore, with her left and right arms bound together, she performs the act of lifting the earth, standing in the *ālīḍha* posture.

In the north is Vetālī, white in color and joyful-faced, with a gaze that raises the dead; she pours down a stream of nectar from a skull-cup and goblet with the luster of moonstone in her right hand, while holding a vajra-banner in her left hand, standing in her preferred posture.
In that very mandala, in the eastern compartment—

Pukkasi is multicolored, with a dancing face and a dancing gaze. With her right vajra-fist, she holds a five-pronged flaming vajra; with her left hand, she holds a *kalpavṛkṣa* creeper shaken by the wind. She performs a dance in the midst of a smoky cremation ground filled with garlands of skulls and other ornaments.

To the right is Caṇḍālī, blue in color, mounted upon a circle of wind (*vātamaṇḍalika*). Her face is full of playful movement and her gaze is directed upward. With her right fist, she grasps a vajra-spear. By holding a cloth of wind and releasing the circle of wind, she causes the object of the rite (*sādhya*) to fall prostrate and so forth.

In the west is Ghasmarī, black in color, with a mouth chewing a corpse and a gaze fixed on devouring. She holds a pit of blazing vajra-fire in her left hand; with her right hand, she grasps a sword in a vajra-fist and stands in the *pratyālīḍha* posture. In the north, she resembles Śrī Heruka in form; holding a skull-cup (*caṣaka*) in her left hand, she carries a *khaṭvāṅga* on her left shoulder. In the south, with her three-fold bannered hand, she holds a five-pronged blazing vajra; she stands upon the feet of Śrī Heruka, possessing two arms and one face.

In the southeast corner is Cāpadhāriṇī, red in color; with her left hand she holds a vajra-bow, and with her right hand, which holds a vajra, she draws the bowstring in the act of shooting vajra-arrows.

In the southwest is Khaṭvāṅgadhāriṇī, adorned with a crown of skulls and a Buddha as the crest-jewel (*cūḍāmaṇi*); she is of a violent yet bright white complexion, and with her right hand she brandishes a five-pronged flaming vajra. In the northwest [=left? she is intent on the threatening gesture (*tarjanī*) with a wrathful fist.

In the northwest (Vāyavya) is Cakradhāriṇī, white-green in color, intent on threatening with her left hand in the *krodhamuṣṭi* gesture, while with the middle finger of her right hand she raises an eight-spoked wheel. In the northeast (Aiśāna) corner is Citrapatākādhāriṇī, gold-stone colored; with her right hand she holds a multi-colored banner (*citrapatākā*) attached to a vessel (*saṃghaṭa?*), and she stands in a *muṣṭi* [gesture] with her left hand. [The goddesses] holding the emblems of flowers, incense, lamps, and perfumes, joined in the *añjali* gesture, are the goddesses of worship known as Aśva, Go, Jā, Sā, Bhūti, and Saṃjñitā.

In the middle of the eastern gate is Turaṅgāsanā, who, with her left hand, holds a lotus raised up with a horse’s head and a green horse; with a vajrāṅkuśa held in her right hand, she draws in the entire family of wrathful deities (krodhakula).
At the western gate is Ālokā, who binds the entire family of wrathful deities by means of a vajrasphoṭa joined with two maṇḍalas of the moon and sun.

At the northern gate is Bhasmapralayavetālī; with her left hand she holds within a skull-cup the image of a Buddha situated upon a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*). With her right hand, by means of the practice of sounding a vajra-bell, she stands subduing the entire family of wrathful deities.
All of these are positioned in the *pratyālīḍha* stance and are endowed with the aesthetic flavor of their respective gazes and expressions.
O Primordial One, Great Being, Great Joy, Great Delight!
O Samantabhadra, Universal Self, Vajra, Vajra of Great Intelligence, Lord! O Mind, Being, Supreme Samādhi, Vajra, Great Holder of the Vajra!
O Samantabhadra, the universal self; O Lord of the pride of the Vajra; O Mind, Being, Supreme Samādhi; O Vajra, Great Holder of the Vajra;
O Supreme Conduct of Samantabhadra; O Māra, Destroyer of Māras!
O All-Awakened One, Great Awakened One, Buddha, first-born of the sons of the Buddhas;
Vajra-Hūṃkāra, Hūṃkāra, Lord of the World, bestower of jewels;
Great Passion, Great Bliss, Desire, Liberation, and Great Wealth.
O you who exist in the three times, the three realms of existence, the three triangles, the summit of the three worlds, and the three elements;
O purifier of the cycle of existence, you who are the source of the stable, the manifest, the subtle, and the accumulation of the gross, and who have attained the excellence of the mobile.
Without beginning or end, appearing at the very start, abiding within all;
the reality of the seal of yoga and the commitment, the great festival of truth;
the Tathāgata of great accomplishment, the great wise one of the activity of Dharma.
Protector of the true Dharma and virtuous deeds, awakener of the mind of enlightenment;
Vajra-wrath, great wrath, terrifying with flames at the end of the eon;
supreme subduer of the wicked, destroyer of all that is fierce.
Utterly pure Great Lotus, the great method of wisdom and skillful means;
through the purity of passion, the supreme samādhi, the Great Lord of universal passion;
the eternal reality of infinite space, the great abode of all beings.
O Lord of Splendor, O King who fulfills all hopes!
Homage be to you, homage be to you, homage be to you—homage again and again!
I am your devotee; I take refuge in you. O Vajrasattva, grant me success this very day!
One should recite this King of Hymns every day;
the attainment of the Dharma-vāra-sakṛnnāda will become very swift. Furthermore, if one desires accomplishments (*siddhi*), they will occur daily at the morning twilight.
Having offered praise, one is liberated from all sins and attains accomplishment in the pure realms.
By turning [the wheel of the mantra] even once, it constantly removes all suffering and increases good fortune, glory, and the perfection of wealth in all accomplishments. (= Paramādya D 205v–206r)

Then, having summoned, caused to enter, bound, and brought under control the Blessed One together with his retinue upon that imagined mandala-ground, one should accomplish [the rite] by means of the previously mentioned heart-mantra. Having assumed the vajra-bandha mudrā of the secret goad together with the bell, one should pierce the mouth [of the deity] with the thumb and index finger joined as a vulva, and then press it with the right thumb acting as a lingam. (9.421)
Suratavajra: Having bound the suratavajrā [mudrā], standing within the middle bond, with the thumbs equal and the final vajras [of the fingers] joined, that is the supreme firmness. (9.423abc)
Following the sequence of the two middle [fingers], one should join one's own heart with this [mantra]; thereafter, according to another text,

having performed the expulsion of obstacles with "Oṃ vajrayakṣa hūṃ" while employing the mudrā, and having provided the enclosure and the cage, one should fasten the doors with the Vajramuṣṭisamayamudrā and the Vajrarakṣamudrā.

"Oṃ vajrarakṣa haṃ"—with this, one should perform all protections. Having formed a vajrāñjali with the two index fingers bent, one should hold them at the two secret places and the mouth; this is the Vajrayakṣa mudrā.

Regarding the Vajramuṣṭi-samayamudrā: having joined the thumbs and the final [little] fingers together in the vajra-bind, and having made the two index fingers into a joined needle, one holds it at the heart; this is the Vajrarakṣa mudrā.
Then, having bowed to the Blessed One and offered an *argha* to the Blessed One and his retinue with the mantra "haḥ haḥ haḥ hoḥ rulu rulu huṃ," he should bind the *samaya-mudrā* of Śrī Heruka.

"Haḥ haḥ haḥ rulu rulu huṃ. Having thus visualized the object of sight together with its retinue, one should say: "Jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ! You are the pledge; I am the pledge! Haḥ haḥ haḥ [4] haḥ haḥ haḥ rulu rulu huṃ! Thus one should visualize.
Having propitiated [the deity] together with his retinue, he should again propitiate him together with his retinue by means of the Vajramudrā, uttering "HA" and that same general heart-mantra.
The Vajra-Ṣaḍaṅguli-mudrā with the hands opened upward and the fingers separated and slightly bent, with the two thumbs wide apart, is the Karālavajra Yakṣiṇī;
this is the Śrī-Vajrayakṣa-mudrā, O Blessed One, which is the samaya-mudrā for [the deity] together with his retinue. [6]
Having formed the *vajramudrā*, with the middle fingers thus contracted, it is indeed called *vajravajrā* because of the supreme *vajra* of desire (*kāmāgravajra*) of the middle [finger].

This is the *śrīvajrahṛdayamudrā*. The *mudrā* arising from *vajrabandha* and originating from the primordial *vajra* should hold the two middle fingers at their tips, not touching one another; this becomes the divine *madhyākāmāgravajra*. Having visualized a blazing *vajra* in one’s own heart with the syllable *HŪṂ*, while uttering that very *HŪṂ*, one should bind the *samayamudrā*. Then, as before, one should visualize a *vajra* upon one’s own tongue.

"O Goddess, you are *subhagā* (fortunate), I am *hir*," thus [one should say]. Having placed the common *dharmamudrā* upon the tongues of all the deities with [the mantra] *iti*, one then [places] the specific form of awakening,
namely *seyaṃ hīr*, for Śrī Heruka.
"Hrīḥ" belongs to Gaurī;
"jrīḥ" belongs to Cauryā; and "śīḥ" belongs to Pramohā.
*Jiḥ* belongs to Vetālī;
*huṃ phaṭ* belongs to Pukkasī, Caṇḍālī, Ghasmarī, and those who assume the form of Śrī Heruka;
and *may* belongs to the bearer of the noose (*yoṇa*).
"Vaṃ" belongs to the goddess holding a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga); "Yaṃ" belongs to the goddess holding a wheel (cakra); "Raṃ" belongs to the goddess holding a variegated banner (citrapatākā).
The syllable *a* for the flower offering; the syllable *ā* for the incense offering;
*am* for the lamp offering.
Aḥ is for Gandhā;
the syllable Jaḥ is for Turaṅgamā;
the syllable Hūṃ is for Vajrapuṣpī.
One should place the syllable BAṂ on Vajrālokā and the syllable HOḤ on Sarvakāmalatā upon the tongue.

Having emanated a universal vajra in one's own heart with the syllable *Aḥ*, one should cause the Blessed One together with his retinue to enter the action-seal (*karmamudrā*), while reciting the general heart-mantra as it has been taught:
*Hūṃ vajrakāmukaśarāya namaḥ śrīrāgavajra samaya namaḥ*.
"Obeisance to Khaṭvāṅgavajrapralaya;
obeisance to Śrīvajraghaṇṭacalana.
Reciting thus, [one should worship] the goddesses on the left and the right.
"May all eat together; may all living beings enjoy whatever food they have.

With these words from the *Devīgīta*, one extends the two little fingers of both hands in the *vajramuṣṭi* gesture; that is the *śrīherukamuṣṭi*. By means of this, one should personally perform the *mahāmudrā* gesture for Śrī Heruka along with his retinue.
This is the *karmamudrā* of Akṣavaśya together with his retinue.
Then, as before, having visualized a five-pronged blazing vajra at one’s own heart,
one should seal it with various diverse, whirling glances.
Having deluded [them] with various and manifold kisses and embraces,
and having feasted [them] on various and manifold enjoyments of every pleasure,
O Aho, display the various and manifold *saṃvara*. (9.102)
Having deluded the mudrā, consume her!
Entering great bliss, *hūṃ*, he illuminates it.
*Ala la la la hoḥ*, manifesting transformations!

One should chant the song: "By means of the nets born of the yoga of transformations" (9.103). Likewise, having performed a dance with both the right and left hands, one should form the *mahāmudrā* by means of the prescribed gestures of the eight arms of the Blessed One Śrī Heruka, [the hands] reaching down to the tip of the *khaṭvāṅga* in the manner of the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*).
With a skull-cup in the left hand and the right hand in the triple-bannered gesture (tripatākā), which is the mudrā of space, the yogin becomes a wanderer through all space;
from space, he brings forth all the excellent jewels, such as women and so forth, and all musical instruments.
Having sealed with this mudrā and by means of the gesture of casting down, one who casts everything down easily from the state of bliss indeed enjoys all sleep and enjoyment;
he protects the inexhaustible host of ḍākinīs, including Rudra, Indra, Upendra, Candra, and Ārka. (9.83)
Having cast [them] down by his own power, he devours them entirely through his illusory powers.
This is the mudrā named *Śrīvajrasattva-Ḍākinī-samvara*, blessed by the union with the equality of all space.
She has one face and two arms; this is the second great mudrā (*mahāmudrā*) of the sixteen [deities] beginning with Śrīgaurī, whose scent is like this.
"Peisa? He who is equal toward all,
he who is a friend to all living beings"—
having performed the dance according to this very verse previously mentioned, the great seals (mahāmudrās) must be affixed exactly according to the written record.
Even the horse-riders and other gatekeepers must perform a dance to the song of the Goddess and bind the great mudrās. Then,
with the sounds of "sūtkāra" from the tasting [of the nectar], they shall dry up even the three worlds by means of the sprinkling of Rudra, the Moon, the Sun, and Yama (9.30).

Thus, with the whistling sounds of those who relish the pleasure of the Rāsa dance— sounds that include Rudra, Indra, Upendra, Candra, Arka, Yama, and Matsya— the Goddess Turaṅgamā shall destroy the three worlds. (9.31)
Thus [is the mantra] of Vajramukhī.
With the gaze of tasting, one may devour even the three worlds, together with Rudra, Indra, Upendra, the Moon, the Sun, Yama, and Matsaka. (9.32)
Thus [ends] the *Vajrāloka*.

Even one who possesses a body along with Rudra, Indra, Upendra, the Moon, and the Sun— consisting of the essence of all— and who is composed of the savoring of the self of all, would bring [the world] back to life (9.33).
Thus ends the "Great Seal" (mahāmudrā) of the Ash-Bhairava Vetālī.

All these great seals, together with their respective insignia, are red and possess mandalas with the appearance of flames; they are to be employed with the general heart-mantra or with their own specific mantra. Whichever seal one should bind, for whichever great being.
While reciting the mantra, one should meditate on that [deity] as one's own self by means of the heart-mantra.
This is the commitment (*samaya*) of all mudrās;
by meditating on one's own Great Mudrās (*mahāmudrā*), one shall accomplish all siddhis.
"In the family of the Tathāgata as well, this is the most excellent accomplishment for the fortunate. This is the rule regarding the *dharmatā* of all families.

Then, as before, having consecrated the Blessed One and having consecrated Śrī-Gaurī and the others with the skull-cup consecration (*kapālābhiṣeka*), and with the mudrā of Śrī-Heruka; then, if possible, having offered the *argha*, one should recite the general heart-mantra for the Blessed One together with his retinue, using the five offerings beginning with external flowers.

Having performed worship together with the mudrās as before, one should contemplate the Viśvavajra within one’s own heart. First, one should perform the fourfold secret worship beginning with the wrathful weapons; then, having bound the action-mudrā (karmamudrā) of Śrī Heruka and so forth, [one recites]:
"O you who desire the drum, O giver of divine [attainments], supreme Tathāgata, grant me siddhi! Oṃ hūṃ. (6.63) "The supreme Tathāgata shall attain siddhi! Oṃ hūṃ. (6.64)
"May my *samayin* be perfected—*unnamu* (*6.65*)—may the Great All-Wine be perfected, *oṃ hūṃ*; may the Great All-Wine be perfected, *oṃ hūṃ* (*6.66*).
Having performed the dance with this song, [he continues].
Having performed graceful movements according to the impulses of possession,
one should offer all worship with the *piṇḍalika* dances;
indeed, by means of the playful movements of the left and right hands, the tips of which are gracefully danced.
The rite for all offerings and bali consists of the vajrāñjali with palms opened upward.
(8.23) With this mudrā, one should perform a dance with the movements of entering the cremation ground; beautiful with the vajra-louder laughter, one should present all offerings. (8.24)
"Vajrāṭṭahāsa"—this is the general heart-mantra; one should utter it. And by this application, one should offer flowers and the other articles:
"The upward tossing, the downward tossing, the whirling, and likewise the smearing;
these initiate the worship of flowers, incense, lamps, and foremost perfumes. (8.30)
Thus it is said.
Then one should worship with the mudrās of musical instruments:
the wind instrument, the stringed instrument, the percussion instrument, and likewise the solid instrument.
The musical instrument mudrās have been taught as accomplishing all activities.
Even without musical instruments, they are accomplished through the movements of possession and dancing;
however, when accompanied by musical instruments, they are exceedingly effective in all activities, and glory increases fourfold. (9.295–296)
Through the heart-mudrās, mantras, and vidyās, there are indeed various ritual actions;
by means of the Viṣkambhikā and other rites, all siddhis are accomplished.

This is what is meant: one should worship the Blessed One together with his retinue by means of the four musical instruments (*vādya*) as previously described, using the syllables of the general *hṛdaya*. Then, the syllables of the *dharmamudrā* for all the deities; then, the specific syllables of the *dharma* beginning with the syllable *hīḥ*; then, the mantras beginning with the nature of Śrī Heruka; and then, having performed the recitation of the Vidyā of Vajrakumāra, one should worship and utter the syllables of the musical instruments of Śrī Heruka along with his retinue.
In this regard, these syllables are: *ve ko krom*.
Uttering the five *koṃ* syllables together with the single syllable *dhai*, one should invoke the nature of Śrī Heruka.
With *dhai vajra vajra*, [one invokes] the nature of Śrī Gaurī. Again, uttering the five *koṃ* syllables preceded by the syllable *dhai*, [one invokes] the nature of Caurī.
"huṃ bhyo huṃ bhyo"—this is the nature of Pramohā;
"huṃ bhyo huṃ bhyo"—this is the nature of Vetālī;
"huṃ bhyo huṃ bhyo huṃ bhyo"—this is the nature of Pukkasī.

"Rulu rulu hūṃ bhyo"—this is the nature of Caṇḍālī. Then, uttering the five *koṃ* syllables preceded by the syllable *dhai*, it is the nature of Ghasmarī. Again, pronouncing the five *kauṃ* syllables preceded by the syllable *dhai*, it is the nature resembling the form of Heruka.
And [it is] of the nature of the eight, beginning with the sharp arrow (tīkṣṇabāṇa) and so forth; and "ṭāt," "kiṃ," "huṃ," and "ja" are for the horse and so on.
And this knowledge of the musical instruments and mudrās is to be known from those things that are to be known.
Now follows the description of the fourfold secret worship of the weapons of wrath and so forth.
Reciting the song beginning with "Hūṃ! O Vajra-bow and arrow... (9.353a), he should utter it.
"By means of the two playful movements of the tips of the three-fingered gesture (*tripatākā*) at the mouth," thus it is said regarding the releasing;
"the Vajra-dance with the tip whirled like a flash of lightning"—that is how it is remembered.

Having bound that [mudrā], saying "O Vajrarati, [I am] the heart of passion," one should bind her as the *karmamudrā*. One should bind [it] for Śrī Heruka. Then, with the two fists of the wrathful weapon, one should utter "Jaḥ! and "Vajradṛṣṭi-sāyaka" (the arrow of the vajra-gaze).

Having likewise performed the dance, one should bind the *karmamudrā* of Mahārativajrī with "HŪṂ" for the sake of sexual bliss (*surata*). Then, for Śrī Heruka; then for Kelīkilā with "HŪṂ VAJRAKELĪKILE HŪṂ," having likewise performed the dance. Then for Locanā’s *karmamudrā* with "OṂ VAJRALOCANATI. Then for Śrī Heruka; then for Snehavajrā with "YAṂ VAJRIṆI SMARARATITI."

Having likewise performed the dance, one should bind the action-seal (karmamudrā) of Mahāśrī with "Mahāśrīvajri hīḥ. Then, for Śrīheruka, [one binds it] with "Hīḥ"; for Karmasvarī, with "Trām"; and for Vajrakāmeśvarī, one should bind the action-seal with "Trām. This is the fourth secret worship.

The *karmamudrā* of *Vajrāstrā* consists of the forceful upward release and casting with both *krodhamuṣṭi*s. The *mudrā* of *Vajrakelīkilā* is the application of the upward raising of two vajras. The *mudrā* of *Snehavajrā*, characterized by the two *śuddhayābhitaya*s, is the upward raising of the two inner palms. The *mudrā* of *Vajragarbhā* is the upward raising of the two hollows. Having performed a prostration of the head by turning the two *krodhamuṣṭi*s in a circular motion at one's own heart and placing them upon the crown of the head, and then lowering them while performing the yoga of spreading the outstretched palms with the thumbs joined in a movement of casting and withdrawing, this is the *mudrā* for flowers, incense, lamps, and perfumes.

Then, having performed the fourfold prostration, one should again bow with this [mantra]: "By means of drawing up the left eyebrow, and by uttering 'ru-lu-ru-lu-lā-pi' with force, one shall cause the three worlds—including the lords of the yakṣas, Upendra, and Rudra—to bow down. (8.7)

Thus. Again, having bound the Mahāmudrā of the Blessed One and having placed the syllable *HŪṂ* in the center of the vajra within one's own heart, one should extend [the mantra] *bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*, which is joined with the four Māras, adorned by the *vinivṛtti*, and perfected as it is projected through universal pervasion. (= 6.26)
The wise one who is *bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svaḥ*,
the bestower of *bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svaḥ*,
the bringer of prosperity in *bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svaḥ*.

One should utter "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ sidhya me" and "Huṃ. All [actions], such as making, restraining, seizing, kissing, and so forth, are the tasting of the bliss of yoga, all of which are joined with the knowledge of the yoga-mudrās. Having ascertained that the entire state of all things, both stable and moving, is the state of yoga and the self, one realizes that everything has the characteristic of space, and through dissolution, even space is without characteristics.
The existence of the entire world is seen to be like a dream and like a reflection; it is seen and touched as if it were a magical illusion on all sides, yet it is not apprehended at all. (9.231–232)

Thus, with the thought, "I shall bring about the unification of the Great Being with Śrī Heruka, who is joined in yoga and is a host of the unsubdued," one should perform the recitation for the sake of the mantra-japa with the words:
*vajrarudramahāsaṃvāsamārutagaluyā meghaghūrṇitagambhīrarasitair ulurulāpitaiḥ*. (9.289)

Having placed "haḥ haḥ haḥ haḥ rulu rulu hūṃ" in the center of the flame-seal (jvālāmudrā) residing in the hearts of all the deities, one should meditate upon oneself as non-different from all the deities and utter this very [mantra]. One should form the resolve: "I shall [attain] the state of being [realized] through the flames of the heart-mantras of my own recitation, which are the foremost of all deities. In this way, all accomplishments (siddhi) are achieved.
Thus, by this, the practice of the heart-mantras of all the deities has been explained; or else, one may recite the mantra.
Oṃ Herukavajra, and so forth.

In the case of the Gaṇasambhava [mandala], however, the heart-mantra of all the deities should be recited by everyone, or else one's own mantra. The dharma-syllables of all the deities, or the dharma-syllables of one's own deity, should be recited according to the application of one's own sādhana. The action-mudrā or the pledge-mudrā should be accomplished as prescribed.

Then, one who desires to accomplish the yoga of Atike, having meditated upon the union with all goddesses as being omnipresent and having attained identity with the bliss of the Great Vajradhara, should exhort himself as Śrī Heruka with this song: "May he,
who is worshipped by the great purities of the lotuses of passion and delight through many various forms of love, manifest [himself] through the bliss of the supreme, eternal yoga."
Having practiced bliss, he who consists of supreme bliss, who is fortunate through the supreme yoga of great bliss, the supreme one of delight—O Rāmaṇa, Hoḥ! Delight in your own commitments! (6.33)
The goddesses are faultless and eternal because they are their own commitment; they are the supreme secret and most excellent. (6.34)

The *samaya*—which consists of all states of existence (*bhava*) and all stable and moving phenomena, like a canvas clearly manifesting the world with its various and diverse conceptions; which is the bliss of yoga for the sons of all the Victors; and which is the *ḍākinī* who bestows [liberation]—is indeed wonderful! Ah!
"O Damayanti, accomplish for me the great, supreme, and eternal accomplishment" (6.35).
As for the goddesses, however, the previously mentioned *nagīti* verses are to be recited by the yoginīs at the birth of the Gaṇas.

If he wishes to perform the recitation (*japa*), he should take the flaming vajra with his left hand in the Śrīheruka fist, and taking the rosary with his right hand, he should hold it against his heart and perform the recitation for the sake of the mantra. Within one month, until the number reaches one hundred thousand, he will become preeminent in purgation (*vireka*). Then, on the full moon night, he should perform the recitation throughout the entire night; thus, the accomplishment of all activities (*sarvakarmasiddhi*) occurs.

Having visualized the flower as the form of Gaurī and having recited the mantra over it, to whomsoever one gives it, that person becomes sealed. One should visualize the incense as the form of Caurī, the lotus as the form of Pramohā, the water as the form of Vetālī, the tree and creeper as the form of Pukkasī, the garment as the form of Caṇḍālī, and the fire as the form of Ghasmarī; having visualized these and recited the mantra over them, to whomsoever one gives them, that person becomes sealed.

Again, one should contemplate oneself as having become one with the sādhya through the yoga of the form of Gaurī; in this way, one seals [the sādhya]. Having held a hook with one’s own mantra, one should draw the heart of the sādhya by means of the yoga of Caurī, which is like the conflagration at the end of an aeon; in this way, there is the drawing of the heart. Having entered the body of the sādhya through the yoga of Pramohā and having become one with him, one should contemplate oneself; in this way, he becomes deluded.

One should mentally sprinkle [the subject] with the water of immortality through the *vetālī*-yoga; thus one causes the dead to rise. One should mentally snap the fingers through the *pukkasī*-yoga; thus one makes the subject dance. Having become one with the subject by means of the *proṅkṣayaśva*-sādhya, one should take away the life-breaths of the subject through the *caṇḍālī*-yoga and depart; thus one kills. One should mentally devour the subject through the *ghasmarī*-yoga; thus one devours everything.

Gazing at the object of accomplishment (*sādhya*) with a sidelong glance from the left, one should strike the heart of the *sādhya* with arrows issuing forth from that gaze. In this way, through the yoga of Gaurī, one seals [the target]. Having entered his heart, one accomplishes it mentally; having torn out his heart with the left hand, one draws the heart toward oneself through the yoga of Caurī by means of attraction. Through kissing, either mentally or directly, one brings about delusion through the yoga of Pramohā.

By means of the mind, or directly through the *vetālī* yoga, having embraced the object of practice (*sādhya*), one causes the dead to rise. Through the *pukkasī* yoga, one should cause that which has become one with the object of practice to dance; thus one makes it dance. Having become one with the object of practice by means of the mind, through the *caṇḍālī* yoga, one should cause it to have its gaze directed upward, being utterly deluded by bliss; thus one kills. Through the *ghasmarī* yoga, having mentally cast the object of practice into one's mouth, one should chew it; thus one devours it.

Through the yoga of Śrī Heruka, one who recites the common heart-mantra ending in *hūṃ* reduces the target to ashes. Ending in *haṃ*, it effects the protection of the target; ending in *hā*, it makes the target victorious; ending in *hīḥ*, there is the attainment of all glory; ending in *maṭ*, there is delight in everything. If one recites *raḍ*, one obtains all memory. *Sphaḍ* is for the subduing of all. If one recites *phaṭ*, one kills everything. This should be understood to apply likewise through the yoga of Gaurī and the others. Furthermore, by means of the great mudrās of Gaurī and the others, one may perform these eight activities.
Now, I shall specifically proclaim the unsurpassed counter-seals (prati-mudrā) of all these seals, which distinguish the individual nature of every seal,
by means of the arising of the glorious Vajra-Padma through the performance of vajra-songs and dances.
Sealed, deluded, and consumed, [the victim] lives together with the ashes.
(9.132) Now, its characteristic mark is as follows: the glorious one has his left cheek below, while with his right hand...

"Displaying the lotus, the fist, the face, the dance, the neck, and the upward-gazing eyes" (10.10)—thus, visualizing oneself with a form resembling that of Śrī Heruka, one should contemplate oneself as having become one with her through the mantra and the object of accomplishment (*sādhya*). In this way, one becomes a performer of all varieties of mudrās. Other rites as well should be understood in accordance with the Tantra.

Now, if one should desire the great accomplishment (*mahāsādhana*), having performed the service (*sevā*) for exactly one month in that same manner, one should have a cloth painting (*paṭa*) drawn according to the mandala-yoga. In front of it, one should recite the mantra for another full month as prescribed; on the full moon day, one should recite throughout the entire night. Then, at dawn, one becomes like Śrī Heruka.

Now, if one should desire the accomplishment of yoga, one should meditate upon oneself through the yoga of the mandala until one sees, as it were directly, the form of the deity of one's own mandala every day. Then, on the full moon day, having sat in the center of the mandala, one should recite the mantra throughout the entire night. Then, at dawn, one becomes Śrī Herukavajra himself.
This is by means of the yoga of the gaṇa-mandala. In this way, one should perform the recitation or the meditation.

If that mudrā becomes loose, or if one wishes to release it oneself, one should make it firm three times with the hundred-syllable mantra until fatigue arises. When fatigue has arisen, whether standing or sitting, walking or remaining still, laughing or blazing, wherever and however one may be, one should remain established in the presence of the samaya-mudrā of one’s own deity. (2.6)
Whatever sense faculty should proceed along its path, that does not [exist] by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Through the yoga of non-concentration, one should bring forth one's own tutelary deity (*svādhidevatā*). Then, having withdrawn all activity, one enters the temple once more and [visualizes] one's own deity with the *samayamudrā*.

Having set [the deities] within one’s own body by reciting *jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ*, and having likewise performed the recitation (*jāpa*) and meditation, when one wishes to dismiss them at the end of the first watch or the end of the second watch, then once again perform praise, worship, and prostration according to their names; dedicate the merit for the attainment of the desired goal, and while repeatedly reciting "Vajrasattva, Vajrasattva," perform the binding and releasing of all mudrās in their respective places, and urge the Blessed One together with his retinue to depart.
"This entire moving world, from its beginning to its end, is dependent upon passion. O Great Being, become like a diamond so that you may return! (Paramādya D 177v).
Then, one should release a handful of flowers upward with the General Heart Mantra ending in the syllable *muḥ*. Thus, he is dismissed.

Just as the emanated [deities] should enter their own bodies by means of mental application through skillful yoga— having brought the Blessed One together with his assembly and circle into themselves— and remain having recited the hundred-syllable Vajrasattva mantra three times;
so too, every day, one should perform the ritual preceded by the empowerment and other preliminary rites at least once.

Having brought forth the arising of vajra-flames, whatever merit has been accumulated by me through this supreme vidyā, the womb of bliss— by that, may the world become a holder of the vajra (Vajradhṛk).
The *Sādhanopeyikā* of the Blessed Lord Śrī Heruka Bhaṭṭāraka, extracted from the *Ārya-sarvabuddhasamāyoga-tantra*, is completed.
This work is by the venerable teacher Ānandagarbha.
